criteria.name: Elaboration beyond the inciting gimmick
criteria.instruction: High: the story develops texture, consequence, or a secondary layer beyond the single joke or concept that launched it. Low: once the premise or joke is stated, the rest of the piece merely restates or extends the same beat without adding a new dimension (emotional, thematic, or plot).
criteria.rationale: R08 starts as a 'clumsy cadet with a weird dragon' joke but adds real vulnerability and family shame beneath the comedy; R22 layers humor, romantic tension, and desensitization-to-violence onto its isekai premise. By contrast R13 and R20 stay entirely within their opening joke (grumpy horse-curse banter; bureaucratic aliens) without adding a further layer.

criteria.name: Causal escalation
criteria.instruction: Score high when each major beat logically worsens, complicates, or redirects the preceding problem toward a payoff; score low when incidents are merely appended or resolved without buildup.
criteria.rationale: R04 escalates from missed intervention to personal guilt, and R30 chains small accidents into a comic catastrophe; R34 establishes scarcity, threat, and mounting danger before confrontation.

criteria.name: Self-sufficient: no prior installment, source work or link required
criteria.instruction: Ask whether a reader holding only the writing prompt and this text can follow it. Clearly satisfying: every person, relationship and prior event the story leans on is supplied inside the piece. Clearly failing: the story depends on a named source work, an earlier installment, or linked posts to be intelligible - proper nouns and grievances arrive already-loaded, or the text explicitly directs the reader to read something else first. Borrowing a widely known public character is not automatically a failure if the piece supplies what it needs; inheriting a private cast is.
criteria.rationale: R03 (dense .078 / card .915) drops Roper, Corky, Pine, Jed, Burr and Danny plus 'the lobster incident' and 'that grand finale on the ship' with no orientation at all; R18 (dense .056 / card .953) opens by telling the reader to read part one first; R21 (dense .027 / card .814) threads five inline links to previous stories through its dialogue. All three read as confident and detailed at the sentence level, which is what a scorecard can see; none is legible on its own terms. R17 and R29 by contrast hand the reader everything required.

criteria.name: Moral complication
criteria.instruction: Score whether the story complicates the reader’s moral judgment rather than announcing an easy good-versus-evil position. High scores expose hypocrisy, unintended harm, or defensible motives behind troubling behavior; low scores leave ethical conclusions obvious and unexamined.
criteria.rationale: R06, R20, and R33 make apparently good or bad actions morally unstable, while R25 and R35 resolve their ethical material through comparatively simple judgments.

criteria.name: No mutual-knowledge exposition; information arrives under pressure
criteria.instruction: Score how the reader learns what the world is. Clearly satisfying: facts reach the reader because a character needs them, uses them, is hurt by them, or acts on them, and any background is inferable from behaviour. Clearly failing: characters recite to one another facts that both plainly already possess - a policy 'the Ensemble put in place over a century ago', a house rule that the speaker and listener have both lived under for decades - or the narration halts to brief the reader on history it could have shown.
criteria.rationale: R01 (dense .148 / card .985) has Regalis and Typhon rehearse the Treaty of Silence and the Ensemble's century-old policy at each other, and R10 (dense .101 / card .922) has Randy explain the haunted house's business model and rules to a resident ghost. Both read as fully populated scenes with conflict, dialogue and a twist, which is why a criterion bank ranks them near the top. Against these, R29 conveys the guild's entire rule set by having hatchlings eat two initiates on the page, and R08 reconstructs its mission sideways through what the narrator cannot stop replaying.

criteria.name: Recontextualizing ending
criteria.instruction: Score high when the ending meaningfully changes how earlier details are understood or completes a prepared implication; score low when it merely stops, repeats the premise, or adds an arbitrary final line.
criteria.rationale: R20’s final message reframes the apparent horror, R31’s later transformation reinterprets the bite, and R36’s wedding scene exposes the narrator’s continuing danger.

criteria.name: Functional sensory detail
criteria.instruction: Score whether concrete sensory and physical details do more than decorate the scene. High scores use texture, sound, smell, or bodily action to reveal danger, mood, setting, or character; low scores use generic description or clutter with no narrative function.
criteria.rationale: R11, R22, and R34 make rooms, bodies, and objects carry emotional or plot information; R17 and R25 rely more heavily on abstract explanation and generic scene description.

criteria.name: Distinctive narrating idiom, scored with mechanics disregarded
criteria.instruction: Deliberately set aside spelling, grammar, punctuation, typography, second-language constructions and formatting. Ask only whether the narration has a consistent, particular idiom - diction, rhythm, a characteristic move - that could not be swapped for another narrator's, and whether it holds for the whole piece. Clearly satisfying: a voice you could pick out of a lineup, maintained end to end. Clearly failing: neutral correct prose with no fingerprint, or a voice that starts distinctive and quietly reverts to default narration. Do not reward roughness; simply do not let it decide the score.
criteria.rationale: This is a direct correction for what the scorecard appears to over-weight. R14 (dense .846 / card .024) is misspelled throughout - alieans, habital, ceentury, preverbial - yet sustains a specific mock-lecture debunking voice; R33 (dense .918 / card .127) is lowercase and comma-spliced but its drowsy petulant register is unmistakable; R34 (dense .921 / card .144) carries typos and an apology for non-native English while marching from Caesar to Da Vinci to Wozniak to a ringing telephone. Against these, R30 (dense .142 / card .930) and R25 are clean, correct and anonymous. Mechanics are trivially scoreable by a criterion judge; idiom is not.

criteria.name: Distinctive character voice
criteria.instruction: Score how clearly diction, rhythm, dialogue, and narration distinguish the characters and remain consistent with them. High scores make speakers identifiable without tags; low scores make everyone sound interchangeable or communicate mainly through exposition.
criteria.rationale: R18, R29, and R36 use strongly differentiated voices to carry comedy and characterization; R08 and R17 have dialogue that mainly states information or the joke.

criteria.name: Productive restraint / ambiguity
criteria.instruction: High: the story withholds explanation at a key moment and that withholding deepens meaning or productively unsettles the reader. Low: the story spells out its own logic or punchline in full, leaving nothing for the reader to complete, or any ambiguity present reads as unintentional confusion rather than a considered choice.
criteria.rationale: R03 ends on the unexplained, understated 'Maybe I didn't deserve to,' and R30 never resolves whether the coma or the dream-world is the real one. By contrast R37 fully explains its own joke's mechanics line by line ('An animal that possesses body features...'), leaving no ambiguity or work for the reader.

criteria.name: Concrete sensory/physical grounding
criteria.instruction: High: the story renders action through specific bodily sensation, sound, or physical detail (what a character feels, hears, touches) rather than abstract summary of what happened. Low: events are reported at a summary level ('X happened, then Y happened') without physical texture.
criteria.rationale: R06 grounds the dragon-taming in tactile specifics (harness sliding over a wet-slick face, weight crushing into hot sand); R38 renders taste and bodily horror concretely. By contrast R21's classroom chaos and R27's backstory are relayed through secondhand dialogue summary rather than physically rendered scenes.

criteria.name: At least one invented rule or institution drives the scene
criteria.instruction: Ask whether the piece contains a specific practice, economy, law, procedure or custom that is not standard issue for its genre, and whether the scene actually turns on it. Clearly satisfying: an invented rule with consequences, such that removing it would collapse the scene. Clearly failing: the setting is assembled entirely from off-the-shelf furniture - tavern, hooded bandit, witch's curse, ominous mage upstairs, magic healing stream - and the invented material is limited to proper nouns. Judge invention, not exoticism: an invented rule can be mundane.
criteria.rationale: R17 (dense .972 / card .170) is built on 'first exposure-first extinction' and pays it off with an interstellar conference deciding to go quiet; R29 (dense .947 / card .066) turns on a guild rule against helping hatchlings out of the shell that is enforced by hatchlings eating initiates; R26 turns on the termination fee. Against these, R04 (dense .067 / card .932) is dwarf, witch's curse, magic stream, and R12 (dense .189 / card .982) is tavern, ogre-blooded bouncer, mysterious patron - both immaculately competent and both inventing nothing. Prompt-adherence and coherent-worldbuilding criteria mark genre defaults as passes.

criteria.name: Formal/structural risk that serves the content
criteria.instruction: High: the story takes a deliberate risk with form (a found document, an in-universe official register, a dialogue-only scene, verse-like line breaks) and that form does real work for the content. Low: the story uses a default straightforward scene-then-ending shape with no formal experimentation.
criteria.rationale: R25 is written as an in-universe scholarly survival-guide excerpt, letting it deliver worldbuilding with ironic distance; R28 is told entirely through Socratic dialogue that mirrors its quantum-theory subject; R12 uses minimalist line-broken prose to enact numbness. Compare the conventional scene-plus-punchline shape of R16 or R29, which take no formal risk.

criteria.name: Psychological contradiction
criteria.instruction: Score high when a character’s motives, feelings, or self-image conflict in specific, credible ways; score low when characters have one plainly stated motive with no inner friction.
criteria.rationale: R01 and R31 derive force from narrators whose self-justifications conflict with their actions; R36 similarly complicates protective love with murderous obsession.

criteria.name: Narrative economy
criteria.instruction: Score high when nearly every included detail develops character, setting, tension, or payoff; score low when the piece contains digressions, promotional material, repetition, or ornamental information that does not advance the story.
criteria.rationale: R14 and R32 devote most of their text to framing or meta-commentary, and R40 compresses the premise into disconnected chat fragments; R04 and R28 demonstrate denser narrative use of detail.

criteria.name: Institutional community framing
criteria.instruction: Count references to moderators, subreddit challenges, official contests, community rules, or result announcements. High means the text is embedded in platform institutions; low means it is an ordinary standalone submission.
criteria.rationale: Institutional proximity can alter how a post is contextualized without improving its fiction. R03 is explicitly a response to a moderator challenge, and R24 is formatted as an official contest-results announcement. Posting time, thread position, and whether the story was early under the prompt leave no reliable textual fingerprint here and are discarded.

criteria.name: Inline links and continuation markers to the author's earlier instalments
criteria.instruction: Count references inside the story body (not the sign-off) to the author's own prior work: an explicit 'this is a continuation of [link], read part 1 first' header, hyperlinks to earlier posts embedded in the narration or dialogue, a numbered instalment or posting-streak count, a named shared universe, or characters, places and props used as if the reader already knows them. Score high when there is a part-1 pointer or two or more inline links to previous stories; score low when the piece stands alone and every proper noun is introduced in-text.
criteria.upstream_parent: series momentum and a returning readership carried over from earlier instalments
criteria.rationale: R13 opens 'This is a continuation of [another story], for a picture by the same artist. This will make more sense if you read part 1 first' and depends on Alice/Elise/406 being already known. R30 embeds five hyperlinks to the author's own previous prompt responses inside the dialogue and closes 'This is story #1385 in a row... part of an ongoing saga... all collected at this link'. Readers arriving with prior investment respond to the instalment rather than to the text; if anything the fingerprint makes the standalone piece weaker (unintroduced referents), so it is predictive without being evidence of quality.

criteria.name: Copyedit-level consistency
criteria.instruction: Count consistency of spelling, grammar, punctuation, tense, and paragraph conventions; high means very few surface deviations, low means repeated typos, agreement errors, or unstable conventions.
criteria.upstream_parent: professional status or access to editing help
criteria.rationale: Professional or assisted editing can make presentation appear authoritative without changing the underlying ideas or plot. R09 and R26 maintain unusually consistent formal prose, whereas R22 contains recurring spelling and agreement errors; the same professional background could also genuinely improve writing.

criteria.name: Direct-address paratext / meta notes outside the fiction
criteria.instruction: Look for bracketed or otherwise marked commentary in the author's own voice, addressed to the reader, that sits outside the story's fictional frame: a writer's note before the story, 'thanks for reading,' an apology/edit note, or an emoji sign-off. HIGH = one or more such asides present anywhere in the post. LOW = the post contains only the story text responding to the prompt, nothing addressed to the reader.
criteria.upstream_parent: author's degree of habituation to this community's posting conventions (how many times they have posted here before)
criteria.rationale: R08 opens with an italicized 'Off-topic writer's note'; R07 closes with 'Well...that was fun :) Thanks for reading!'; R12 closes with an apologetic 'Edit: Not my first language...'. All are paratext, not story content, and reflect community fluency rather than the story's craft.

criteria.name: Author self-promotion footer plugging a personal subreddit
criteria.instruction: Count promotional or reader-addressed furniture appearing after the story's last narrative sentence: a link or handle for the author's own subreddit/blog, 'thanks for reading', 'check out my sub', 'like what you read? want to see more?', an invitation to follow, or a claim about the author's other work. Score high when there is a named self-hosted venue plus an explicit call to action; medium when there is a bare 'thanks for reading' or a naked handle with no link; low when the text ends on the story's final narrative line with nothing addressed to the reader.
criteria.upstream_parent: the author has an established personal following they are actively recruiting to
criteria.rationale: R01 ends with a divider then 'Thanks for reading! I have a couple of popular stories... at r/AuthorKurt'; R10 ends '*Like what you read? Want to see more? Check out my sub at /r/Romanticon*'; R03, R13, R30, R32, R38 and R06 all carry the same appended plug. The plug sits outside the fiction and cannot make the prose better, so it is not evidence of quality, but it reliably marks writers who already have an audience here. Marked mixed because the same parent (an audience built over many posts) plausibly also means a more practised writer. Note the channel fires on BOTH halves of the slice (R01/R03/R32/R38 dense-high, R06/R10/R13/R30 dense-low), which is exactly what a reception-side rather than quality-side channel should do.

criteria.name: Self-positioning disclaimers
criteria.instruction: Count explicit claims of inexperience, weak language ability, mediocrity, or requests for correction and advice. High means the author frames the work through visible insecurity or novice status; low means no such self-positioning appears.
criteria.upstream_parent: author reputation or seniority in the community
criteria.rationale: Readers may infer author status from these cues, although experience can also improve the writing itself. R01 calls the story “mid-grade,” R05 says English is not the author’s first language, and R30 describes the author as new to creative writing.

criteria.name: Dialogue-first opening within first two lines
criteria.instruction: Check the opening two lines of the story. HIGH = the story opens directly with quoted spoken dialogue, before any scene-setting narration. LOW = the story opens with descriptive/expository narration, with dialogue (if any) appearing later.
criteria.rationale: R06, R11, R13, R15 and R16 all open on a line of quoted dialogue with zero preceding scene-setting; this is a compositional habit for grabbing attention quickly, not evidence of narrative quality.

criteria.name: Document or chat framing
criteria.instruction: Classify whether the story is presented as a transcript, message exchange, report, extract, or labeled dialogue log; high means a strong non-prose container, low means continuous conventional prose.
criteria.rationale: A novel container can make a piece stand out and clarify its genre before its content is evaluated. R21 presents an italicized protocol extract, R25 uses chat-style quoted messages, and R31 labels speakers as professor and student.

criteria.name: Paragraph-count tally
criteria.instruction: Count how many paragraphs the story has. Score 1.0 when there are many (roughly fifteen or more), 0.5 for a moderate number, 0.0 when there are only one or two. Count the paragraph breaks only; pay no attention to whether anything develops across them.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow structural counterpart of R5A01 'Elaboration beyond the inciting gimmick': paragraph count is the typographic residue of elaboration while measuring nothing about whether the premise is actually developed.

criteria.name: Sentence-final ellipsis count
criteria.instruction: Count how many sentences end in an ellipsis ('...' or '…'). Score 1.0 when several do, 0.5 for one or two, 0.0 for none. Count the punctuation only; pay no attention to what is being left unsaid.
criteria.rationale: PLANTED PROBE (coordinator-authored). Shallow typographic counterpart of R5A06 'Recontextualizing ending': trailing ellipses are the surface mark of an open or suspended close while measuring nothing about whether the ending reframes what preceded it.
